# AI Preview Agent — Inspect The **lens-side nerve center** that lets an external AI agent observe a running Lens. In Lens Studio Preview, it hosts a `postMessage` bridge between the Lens runtime (the Preview panel) and an editor-side plugin, and answers two kinds of request over that bridge: **scene queries** and **orthographic render captures**. This is the universal half of the AI Preview Agent system — it runs on both **SPECS and Snapchat** lenses. The companion `AiPreviewAgentInteract` package adds SPECS-only hand interactions and depends on this one. > Normally you don't wire this up by hand. The editor-side agent tooling > (Core-ChatTools / the `verify-preview` and `preview-inspection` skills) installs the > packed script onto a dedicated **"AiPreviewAgent Handler"** object automatically. Import > this package manually only when authoring/debugging the agent pipeline itself. ## What it does - **Owns the message broker.** `AgentInspectScript` builds a `LensMessageBroker` over a `MessageEvent`, wraps it in a `MessagePublisher` (exposed as the public `publisher` field other packages borrow), and registers handlers. - **`Ping` → `PingResponse`** — liveness heartbeat so the editor knows the handler is alive. - **`RuntimeQuery`** — unified live scene inspection. Four scopes: - `capabilities` — registered component readers, present component types, scene size, schema version - `single` — one object by `uniqueId` - `roots` — top-level scene objects - `filter` — AND-combined predicates (`hasComponents`, `property`, `nearPoint`, `descendantOf`, `nameContains`, `enabledOnly`) with `limit`/`sortBy` and a `filterBreakdown` explaining result-set size - A recursive `ProjectionSpec` controls which fields are returned — cheap fields (name, uniqueId, enabled, parent, childCount, componentTypes) are always populated; `transform` / `components` / `bounds` / `parent` / `children` are lazy. - **`CaptureView` → `CaptureViewResponse`** — orthographic render of a region (framed on a set of `uniqueIds` or a world-space `center`), with `viewAngle` preset, optional `isolate`, and `detail` (low/medium/high). Returns a base64 PNG. - **Deterministic errors** — every failure comes back as `CommandError` with a typed `reason` (`not_found`, `unknown_command`, `invalid_params`, `unknown_component`, `unknown_property`, `internal_error`, `unsupported`, …) when the handler receives and processes a request. A paused or unavailable Preview can still time out. ## Contents | File | Role | |------|------| | `AgentInspectScript.ts` | `@component` entry point — builds broker, registers handlers, owns `publisher` | | `RuntimeQueryHandler.ts` | Resolves `RuntimeQuery` scopes against the live scene | | `ComponentReaderRegistry.ts` | Pluggable readers that serialize component properties (`createDefaultRegistry()`) | | `SceneHelpers.ts` | Scene-graph traversal helpers | | `AABBComputer.ts` | Bounding-box computation for queried objects | | `CaptureHandler.ts` / `OrthoCapture.ts` | Orthographic render capture | | `messaging/` | `LensMessageBroker`, `MessagePublisher`, `Messaging` — subscribe/notify/dispatch-by-type | | `AgentMessages.ts` | Command/response type unions (the wire contract) | ## Dependencies The bridge scripts at the package root (and `messaging/`) import nothing outside this package. `package_dependencies.json` lists InteractionKit, UIKit, Motion and Icons. Those are used by the demo pieces: the `Example/` scripts import `UIKit.lspkg/...` and `InteractionKit.lspkg/...`, and the PLACE_IN_SCENE prefab uses UIKit `Frame` / button components. The bridge only runs in the Lens Studio Preview, on SPECS and Snapchat projects; on device the component does nothing. ## Usage This section ships with the package and describes the installed package. Read it, then follow the links into `Docs/` for the topic you need. It is written for both people and coding agents; generic Lens scripting, scene construction, and Specs spatial design live in the CLAD skills, not here. ### Package identity - Package descriptor: `AiPreviewAgentInspect.lspkg/package.native` (the package version lives there) - Consumer import prefix: `AiPreviewAgentInspect.lspkg/` (flat layout, e.g. `AiPreviewAgentInspect.lspkg/AgentInspectScript`, `AiPreviewAgentInspect.lspkg/AgentMessages`). This is the path `AiPreviewAgentInteract` imports. - Entry point: the `AgentInspectScript` component. - Demo prefab: `AiPreviewAgentInspect__PLACE_IN_SCENE.prefab`. It is self-contained: it carries the guide panel ("Ok, I understood"), the example carousel (minimize) and the `AgentInspectDemo` group with the `AgentInspectScript` object. Drop it into a Specs scene with a Camera and SIK and you get the full demo. The agent tools don't need it. - Demo scaffolding: `AiPreviewAgentInspect.lspkg/Example/` holds the scripts the prefab uses for the guide and the carousel (`ExampleCarousel/`, `GuideDismissPanel/`). They are not part of the bridge; see [components](Docs/components.md#demo-scaffolding-example). - Companion package: `AiPreviewAgentInteract` (SPECS-only hand actions) depends on this one. Nothing here depends on it. ### Version and API status [API status](Docs/api-status.md) lists the current wire commands and the internal helpers. It also records the old per-purpose commands that `RuntimeQuery` replaced. ### Applicability Use this package only to let editor-side agent tools (scene queries, captures) observe a Lens running in the Preview. It is not a runtime scene-query API for Lens logic, and it does nothing on device. Install `AiPreviewAgentInteract` as well when the tools also need to drive SIK hands. Normally the CLAD tools install both for you on an `AiPreviewAgent Handler` object. Never ship it as part of an experience. ### Related CLAD skills - [preview-inspection](https://github.com/lens-studio-devs/ls-extensions/tree/main/plugins/ls-clad/skills/preview-inspection): querying the live Preview and taking orthographic captures through this bridge. - [verify-preview](https://github.com/lens-studio-devs/ls-extensions/tree/main/plugins/ls-clad/skills/verify-preview): the end-to-end QA loop that uses it. - No CLAD? Setup: https://developers.specs.com/docs/clad/setup/setup-ai/ · source: `github.com/lens-studio-devs/ls-extensions`. ### Package Docs (ship in `Docs/`) - [cheat sheet](Docs/cheat-sheet.md) - load-bearing rules; read first - [components](Docs/components.md) - `AgentInspectScript`, publisher, reader registry, wire types - [API status](Docs/api-status.md) - Current / Removed / Internal for this revision - [examples](Docs/examples.md) - manual install and a companion command handler - [troubleshooting](Docs/troubleshooting.md) - no response, duplicate handlers, empty captures ### Verification 1. The project compiles with no errors, and the snippets compile without `as any`. 2. In the Preview, a scene-roots query lists the scene's root objects, and the `AgentInspectScript` object reports the `AgentInspectScript` component type. 3. A capabilities query returns `schemaVersion` "1.0" and the nine registered readers. 4. A capture with `viewAngle` "front" returns a non-empty image of the target. 5. A query with an unknown `uniqueId` returns `null`, not a timeout. ## Manual usage (advanced) Add `AgentInspectScript` as a `ScriptComponent` on any SceneObject. On `onAwake` it sets up the broker and starts answering `Ping` / `RuntimeQuery` / `CaptureView` over the Preview `postMessage` channel. For hand interactions, also add `AgentInteractScript` from `AiPreviewAgentInteract`. It looks for this script on its own object and then up the parent chain, so put it on the same object or on a descendant. Keep a single `AgentInspectScript` per scene (see [troubleshooting](Docs/troubleshooting.md)). ## Built with 👽 by the SPECS team ","version":{"major":4,"minor":0,"patch":0}},{"description":"","id":"8d5a1f87-c2db-4e8c-931f-3bbdffc2f1dd","isInstalled":true,"isUnreleased":false,"name":"package","readme":"# Icons The SPECS iconography set for Spectacles: 353 UI icons mirrored from the SPECS Iconography 3.0 design file and grouped by category, plus an editor plugin that packs only the icons your Lens actually uses into a single optimised atlas. Icons are plain PNG textures, so they drop straight into any material, `Image` component, or script `Texture` input — no runtime library and no setup required. ## Categories | Folder | Icons | | |---|---|---| | `Iconography/Arrows` | 54 | directions, chevrons, turns, undo/redo, upload/download | | `Iconography/System` | 66 | settings, search, lock, visibility, theming, star, share | | `Iconography/Signal-devices` | 34 | wifi, cellular, battery, bluetooth, hotspot, airplane | | `Iconography/Media` | 31 | playback, volume, camera, gallery, microphone | | `Iconography/Input` | 30 | keyboard, keypad, emoji, text size, translate | | `Iconography/Ar-devices` | 32 | Specs, phone controller, hand, cube, globe, tracking | | `Iconography/Editing` | 28 | pencil, brush, crop, palette, sort, transform | | `Iconography/Communication-people` | 25 | users, calls, video, chat, contacts | | `Iconography/Files` | 19 | documents, folders, cloud sync, bookmarks | | `Iconography/Alerts-notifications` | 19 | info, warning, error, checkmark, shield, bell | | `Iconography/Misc` | 15 | infinity, molecule, flask, follow, star | ## Using an icon Drag any icon from `Iconography//` onto a texture slot — a material's Base Texture, an `Image` component, or a `Texture` input on your own script. That is the whole workflow. ```typescript @component export class MyButton extends BaseScriptComponent { @input icon: Texture // assign e.g. Iconography/System/gear.png onAwake() { const image = this.sceneObject.getComponent('Component.Image') as Image const material = image.mainMaterial.clone() image.clearMaterials() image.addMaterial(material) material.mainPass.baseTex = this.icon } } ``` ## Keeping your Lens small Icons that stay in this package are **not** part of your Lens build — only icons your scene references are included. If you use many icons, the bundled **Icon Atlas** plugin packs just those into one texture: 1. Open **Windows › Icon Atlas**. 2. Press **Scan scene for used icons** to see exactly which icons your scene references, and where. 3. Choose a resolution (128 / 160 / 320 px per icon) and press **Create atlas from used icons**. 4. Press **Repoint scene at atlas** to move every reference onto the atlas, so the individual icons are no longer pulled into the build. Step 4 adds a single `IconAtlasBootstrap` component to your scene, which configures the atlas at runtime. Without it, crop regions cannot be applied — Lens Studio only exposes them at runtime. A worked example: 20 icons at 128 px pack into a 640×512 atlas costing about **1.25 MB** of texture memory, against roughly **8 MB** for the same 20 icons loose at their native 320 px. Two things worth knowing: - An atlas reduces **draw calls and asset count**, not bytes — a grid of N icons occupies the same pixels as N separate textures of the same size. The savings come from including only what you use, and from choosing a smaller cell size. - Lens Studio caps imported textures at **2048 px** per axis. The plugin shrinks the cell size automatically to stay inside that and tells you when it does, so an atlas is never silently rescaled. ## Source Icons are generated from the SPECS Iconography 3.0 design file and refreshed automatically. Category folders mirror the sections in that file, so a new section appears here as a new folder. Icon file names are lowercase-kebab and stable — safe to reference from code. The engine layer of the UIKit motion system; UIKit's intent catalog and token library build on it.","id":"042455e3-f10d-4e61-bd5d-bb7f010cb8cd","isInstalled":true,"isUnreleased":false,"name":"package","readme":"# Motion A retained tween engine for Lens Studio: one clock, one live driver per (target, property), timelines, staggers, and scopes. Zero dependencies — no UIKit, no IK; the package imports into any project as-is. The boundary is enforced: `buildSupport/motion-standalone.tsconfig.json` compiles the package alone with no path mappings, so any foreign import is a compile error. This package is the engine only. UIKit's typed intent catalog and token library build on it (`UIKit.lspkg/Scripts/Motion/README.md` covers that layer and the deeper how-to). `Motion.ts` verbs · `Tween.ts` drivers + registry · `Timeline.ts` · `Stagger.ts` · `Channels.ts` · `MotionTicker.ts` clock · `MotionScope.ts` · `Eases.ts` · `MotionTypes.ts` / `MotionValueMath.ts` ## Use it ```ts import {ch} from "Motion.lspkg/Channels" import * as Eases from "Motion.lspkg/Eases" import {Motion} from "Motion.lspkg/Motion" ``` Write a value, no animation: ```ts Motion.set(obj, {channel: ch.alpha, value: 1}) ``` Animate to a value: ```ts Motion.to(obj, {channel: ch.positionY, value: 12, duration: 0.4, ease: Eases.power2.out}) ``` Enter from an offset — the destination is read off the live target, so layout stays the truth: ```ts Motion.from(obj, {channel: ch.alpha, value: 0, duration: 0.3}) ``` Interrupt by just calling again — the property continues from wherever it is: ```ts Motion.to(obj, {channel: ch.positionX, value: 10, duration: 0.5}) Motion.to(obj, {channel: ch.positionX, value: -4, duration: 0.5}) // no cancel, no pop ``` Retarget at high frequency through one retained driver: ```ts const slide = Motion.handle(obj, ch.positionX, {duration: 0.3}) slide(6) // call as often as you like; nothing allocates per call ``` Choreograph with a timeline — author the enter once, exit is the same timeline reversed: ```ts const tl = Motion.timeline({defaults: {duration: 0.3, ease: Eases.power2.out}}) .add(panel, {channel: ch.alpha, from: 0}) .add(panel, {channel: ch.scale, from: new vec3(0.96, 0.96, 0.96)}, {at: "withPrevious"}) tl.play() // enter tl.play(false) // exit ``` ### Reversing, and what an interruption costs `play(false)` / `reverse()` walks the timeline back. If nothing in it is authored per-direction, that is a literal RETRACE: the schedule is mirrored and every tween reads its forward curve, so - a direction change mid-flight is EXACTLY continuous on every channel — no channel moves on the frame you flip, so an interruption never pops, and - coming back undoes in order: whatever ran last runs first. Author a `[reverse, forward]` duration, ease, or position anywhere in the timeline and you are asking for two different schedules over two different curves, which cannot also be continuous. Those fall back to holding the FIRST child exactly (the primary surface in every intent) while the others re-phase. So: reach for per-direction values when the design really does want a different exit, and know that a mid-flight interruption of that timeline will step on the secondary channels. Stagger a cascade: ```ts import {distribute} from "Motion.lspkg/Stagger" const delayOf = distribute(tiles.length, {amount: 0.4, from: "center"}) tiles.forEach((tile, i) => tl.add(tile, {channel: ch.alpha, from: 0}, {time: delayOf(i)})) ``` Loop: ```ts Motion.to(icon, {channel: ch.scaleY, value: 1.08, duration: 0.8, repeat: -1, yoyo: true}) ``` Clean up pooled or recycled targets with a scope: ```ts import {MotionScope} from "Motion.lspkg/MotionScope" const scope = MotionScope.for(row) Motion.from(row, {channel: ch.alpha, value: 0, scope}) scope.revert() // on recycle: kill + restore authored values ``` All together — pop a grid in with overshoot, then flip it: ```ts const pop = Motion.timeline() const popDelay = distribute(tiles.length, {amount: 0.6, from: "center", ease: Eases.power2.in}) tiles.forEach((tile, i) => { pop .add(tile.object, {channel: ch.scale, from: vec3.zero(), duration: 0.55, ease: Eases.back(1.9).out}, {time: popDelay(i)}) .add(tile.object, {channel: ch.positionZ, from: -24, duration: 0.5, ease: Eases.power3.out}, {at: "withPrevious"}) }) pop.play() const flip = Motion.timeline() tiles.forEach((tile, i) => { flip.add(tile.object, {channel: ch.rotationY, from: 0, to: 180, duration: 0.6, ease: Eases.power2.inOut}, {time: i * 0.04}) }) flip.play() ``` ## Multi-step moves: keyframes A move with stops along the way is DATA on one tween, not several tweens taking turns on the same property: ```ts timeline.add(item, { channel: ch.position, from: rest, keyframes: [ {value: midPoint, ease: Eases.power2.out}, // leg 1 {value: finalSlot, duration: 0.5, ease: Eases.power2.in} // leg 2 ] }) ``` - Each entry describes the leg that ENDS at that stop. `duration` and `ease` are per leg; both fall back to the tween's own values, and both accept `[reverse, forward]` pairs like everywhere else. - The tween's `duration` is therefore a per-leg fallback, not the total. The total is the sum of the legs. - ONE tween owns the property for the whole path: `killTweensOf` stops the entire move, `getTweensOf`/`isTweening` report it as one thing, and a scope holds one entry for it. - `reverse()` RETRACES the path. With one ease per leg it is the same curve walked backwards, so the value cannot move when you flip. Give a leg a `[reverse, forward]` ease or duration and reversal renders that leg's own reverse curve instead, with the rendered value solved inside the active leg so the flip still holds its value. - `retarget()` COLLAPSES a path: a redirect has no meaningful set of intermediate stops, so it becomes a straight move from the live value. - A timeline REJECTS a second child on a property one child already animates — keyframes are the way to express that, and the old shape could not be owned, killed, or reversed as a unit. Standalone (outside a timeline) the verb is `Motion.keyframes`, because a tween takes either a destination or keyframes and never both: ```ts Motion.keyframes(material, { channel: Channels.shaderFloat(material, "headPos"), from: 0, keyframes: [ {value: 1, duration: 0.5, ease: Eases.power2.out}, // travel {value: 1, duration: 0.6} // hold, then loop ], repeat: -1 }) ``` That shape is how you build a LOOP with internal structure — travel, hold, rest — which is what a loading sweep needs. A timeline cannot do it: `tick` completes and reports dead, so the ticker drops it, and re-playing from inside `onComplete` is a no-op (the node is still listed, so `add` dedupes, then the walk splices it out). Repeating tweens reset and report alive, so they stay scheduled. Give several drivers the same total duration and they stay in phase — they advance on one shared dt. The UIKit development project's motion showcase is the full version of that last one. Its numeric engine scenarios and keyframe-path coverage live there too (trails make the shape visible: an arc through its stops versus a straight two-point control). ","version":{"major":4,"minor":0,"patch":0}},{"description":"Please refer to the attached README for detailed instructions and information about the InteractionKit (IK).","id":"be230f2e-d00c-4bf5-890e-aba4d64330f9","isInstalled":true,"isUnreleased":false,"name":"package","readme":"# InteractionKit (IK) InteractionKit (IK) is a set of tools, components, and assets designed to simplify the development of interactive augmented reality experiences in Lens Studio. IK provides reusable building blocks to help you create engaging AR content more efficiently. ## Usage These instructions ship with IK and describe the package revision installed in the project. They are written for both people and coding agents; prefer them over package APIs remembered by an external skill, and follow the links into `Docs/` for the topic you need. ### Package identity - Source package descriptor: `InteractionKit/package.native` - Installed package descriptor: `InteractionKit.lspkg/package.native` - Consumer import prefix: `InteractionKit.lspkg/` - Installed primary prefab: `InteractionKit.lspkg/Prefabs/InteractionKit.prefab` - Source prefab: `InteractionKit/Prefabs/InteractionKit.prefab` - UIKit depends on this package for targeting and interaction. ### Version and API status This README and its linked files describe the installed package revision. Read [API status](Docs/api-status.md) before using an older IK example. Use the [Release Notes](https://developers.snap.com/spectacles/spectacles-frameworks/spectacles-interaction-kit/release-notes) for human release history. ### Applicability Use IK for interactors, targeting, gestures, manipulation, interaction events, and the scene infrastructure that makes spatial controls interactive. Use UIKit for themed visual controls, panels, layout, scrolling, text entry, and dialogs. Only documented public APIs are supported. Do not import files under `Core/SpecsInteraction` or runtime-selection helpers used by `HandInteractor`; those are implementation details and may move between package versions. ### Imports and entry points - Import public symbols with the exact `InteractionKit.lspkg/` prefix. - For standard scene setup, instantiate the `InteractionKit` prefab instead of reconstructing its hierarchy. - Use the linked API reference below to select public modules and exports. Do not infer support from a file merely being present in the package. ### Version 4 naming migration The exported package is `InteractionKit.lspkg`. The API entry point is `IK.ts`: ```ts import {IK} from "InteractionKit.lspkg/IK" import type {IKAPI} from "InteractionKit.lspkg/IK" ``` The log provider and component are `IKLogLevelProvider` and `IKLogLevelConfiguration`; access the provider through `IK.IKLogLevelProvider`. Update older package imports and symbol names when adopting version 4. Serialized Inspector field names are unchanged. Importing the renamed archive alongside an existing package can create a second copy. Use a package update/migration workflow that preserves authored components and Inspector values, and verify references before removing an older package. Changing TypeScript imports alone does not migrate scene assets. The development project directory and `.esproj` retain the name `SpectaclesInteractionKit`. The source package is `Assets/InteractionKit`; project-local source imports use the `InteractionKit/` prefix. Lens Studio uses the source package folder name to suggest `InteractionKit.lspkg` when exporting from the Assets panel. `Core/SpecsInteraction` and LensCore API identifiers retain their runtime names. The linked online documentation may still use earlier package/API names; use the source and declarations shipped with this revision for the current names. ### Supported workflows For Asset Library installs: 1. Add Device Tracking to the main camera and set Tracking Mode to `World`. 2. Set Preview's Device Type Override to `Spectacles`. 3. Add the InteractionKit prefab to the Scene Hierarchy. 4. In Project Settings, enable the Spectacles platform and disable unrelated platforms. 5. Build package consumers only after the prefab and camera setup are present; visual components can render while remaining non-interactive when IK scene infrastructure is missing. Starter projects may already provide this setup; inspect before adding a second prefab. ### API reference Use the [IK API Reference](https://developers.snap.com/lens-studio/api/lens-scripting/variables/Packages_SpectaclesInteractionKit_SIK.SIK.html) and public TypeScript declarations shipped with this package. ### Examples Start with the [Get Started Guide](https://docs.snap.com/spectacles/spectacles-frameworks/spectacles-interaction-kit/get-started) and the prefabs and examples shipped with the matching IK release. For visual controls backed by IK, use the examples in the installed UIKit README rather than duplicating UIKit lifecycle guidance here. ### Known limitations - IK scene setup is required for hover and trigger events; missing setup can fail silently while visuals continue rendering. - Required `@input` fields declared without `@allowUndefined` must be wired. Leaving one unwired passes the editor's structural checks but throws at Lens start when the component initializes (`"... was not provided"`), which can take down the whole Lens. Several components in this package declare non-optional inputs this way—`HandVisual`, `InteractorLineVisual`, `InteractableOutlineFeedback`, and `InteractableSquishFeedback` among them. To find the mandatory inputs for any component, read its source and wire every `@input` that lacks `@allowUndefined`. - Preview device override and project platform settings are separate; configure both for representative Spectacles behavior. ### Manipulation and targeting behavior These are version-specific rules for `Interactable` and `InteractableManipulation` in this package revision. Confirm against the installed component source if a behavior looks different. - `Interactable.targetingMode` values are `1` Direct, `2` Indirect, `3` Direct/Indirect (the default), `4` Poke, `7` All. The Poke bit is mutually exclusive with Direct and Indirect. - `InteractableManipulation` needs an `Interactable` on the same SceneObject. Without one it logs `InteractableManipulation requires an interactable to function.` at start and does nothing—the object will not move. Wire an `Interactable` (with a collider) on the same SceneObject as the manipulation. - `InteractableManipulation` is incompatible with Poke targeting. On attach it clears the Poke bit from its host `Interactable.targetingMode` and logs `Poke targeting is incompatible with InteractableManipulation...`. A host left on Poke-only (`4`) then has no targeting mode and cannot be grabbed; a host on All (`7`) keeps only Direct/Indirect. Keep manipulation hosts on Direct/Indirect (`3`) and put poke-only controls on a separate `Interactable` that carries no manipulation. A scene-wide poke interactor does not change this. - `InteractableManipulation` also forces `Interactable.useFilteredPinch = true` on its host. The filter smooths and can delay the transition into the grabbed state, so wire targeting and colliders such that a Direct grab still engages through the delay, and do not assert an exact manipulation state on the first frames of a grab. - `Interactable.enableInstantDrag` (default `false`) controls when a trigger becomes a drag: while `false`, dragging starts only after the interactor's drag threshold is crossed; set it `true` to start dragging immediately on trigger. A manipulation host that plays hover/trigger feedback but never translates under the Preview mouse or a distant ray is usually missing `enableInstantDrag = true`. Re-assert it after replacing the host `Interactable`. - An `Interactable` enables and disables its colliders together with itself and discovers colliders on its SceneObject (via editor wiring, UIKit Element subclasses, or the InteractionManager). Keep one `Interactable` per interactive object so a feedback or affordance child carrying its own `Interactable` does not steal Direct hits from the intended grab host. ### Verification 1. Confirm exactly one IK prefab is active in the Scene Hierarchy. 2. Confirm the main camera uses World device tracking. 3. Run Preview with the Spectacles device override. 4. Exercise every interactor used by the Lens and verify hover, trigger, drag, and release behavior—not just rendering. 5. Resolve TypeScript imports against this installed package revision. ## Documentation and API Reference - **Getting Started**: Learn how to use IK by following the [Get Started Guide](https://docs.snap.com/spectacles/spectacles-frameworks/spectacles-interaction-kit/get-started). - **API Reference**: Explore the full API documentation for IK [here](https://developers.snap.com/lens-studio/api/lens-scripting/variables/Packages_SpectaclesInteractionKit_SIK.SIK). Only documented APIs are supported for Lens scripts. Anything not in the API reference above is an internal implementation detail; its paths and exported TypeScript symbols may change between IK versions. ## Release Notes IK is updated frequently. Stay informed about the latest features and fixes by checking the [Release Notes](https://developers.snap.com/spectacles/spectacles-frameworks/spectacles-interaction-kit/release-notes). ## How to Set Up IK in Your Project ### If Using a Starter Project If you’re starting with one of the provided starter projects, the setup is already configured for you. You can begin building right away. ### If Adding IK from the Asset Library Follow these steps to configure IK in your project: 1. **Add Device Tracking**: Ensure the main camera in your scene has a Device Tracking component with the tracking mode set to World. 2. **Set Device Type**: In the Preview Panel, set the device type override to Spectacles: - Go to the cogwheel in the top-right corner of the Preview Panel. - Select Device Type Override > Spectacles. 3. **Add the Prefab**: Drag and drop the InteractionKit prefab into the Scene Hierarchy. 4. **Set Platform to Spectacles**: In Project Settings > Platform Settings, select Spectacles and unselect other platforms. You’re now ready to start building with IK! ","version":{"major":4,"minor":0,"patch":0}},{"description":"UI Kit (or, simply, UIKit) is a collection of components, prefabs, scripts and assets designed to facilitate the development of graphical user interfaces (GUI) in Lens Studio.","id":"c07d6aba-e866-4b53-abaa-9848ce573786","isInstalled":true,"isUnreleased":false,"name":"package","readme":"# UIKit UIKit is a package of components, utilities, and assets for building interactive spatial interfaces in Lens Studio. It depends on InteractionKit (IK) for targeting and interaction. ## Documentation and API reference - [Get Started Guide](https://developers.snap.com/spectacles/spectacles-frameworks/spectacles-ui-kit/get-started) - [Release Notes](https://developers.snap.com/spectacles/spectacles-frameworks/spectacles-ui-kit/release-notes) ## Usage This section ships with the package and describes the exact installed revision. Read it, then follow the links into `Docs/` for the topic you need.
